title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by order of the Highest Authorities, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, frightened of the name of Napoleon, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
(History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by the historian Bogdanovich.)

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") whom the Russian mind does not acknowledge—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern the higher laws.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of adulation and enthusiasm; he is grand. But Kutuzov—the man who, from the beginning to the end of his activity in 1812, never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, gave an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history, along with a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something indefinite and pitiful, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little ashamed.

And yet it is hard to imagine a historical figure whose actions were so unwaveringly directed toward a single aim. And it would be hard to imagine any aim more worthy or more in harmony with the will of the entire people. Still harder would it be to find another instance in history where the aim of a historical figure was so completely accomplished as the aim to which all of Kutuzov's efforts were directed in 1812.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to the writer Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How was it you promised not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—who then alone amid a senseless crowd understood the whole tremendous significance of what was happening—what did it matter to him whether Rostopchin attributed the calamities of Moscow to him or to himself? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

Not only in these cases but constantly, that old man—who through long experience had reached the conviction that thoughts and the words expressing them are not what move people—used perfectly meaningless words that simply came into his head.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his real thoughts with the bitter conviction that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow is not the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all our maneuvers are useless, that everything is being accomplished of itself better than we could desire, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge", that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

And this courtier, as he is portrayed—who lies to Arakcheev to please the Emperor—he alone, at the cost of the Emperor's displeasure, said in Vilna that to carry the war beyond the frontier was useless and harmful.

Nor do his words alone prove that only he understood the meaning of the events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to brace all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of our people and our army.

This procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This same Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz had predicted it would be lost, alone and against everyone else declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite generals' assurances that the battle was lost, and despite the unprecedented fact that an army had had to retreat after winning it. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that battles, which were useless then, should not be fought, and that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events, now that they and their results lie before us, provided we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people.
But how did that old man, alone, in opposition to the general opinion, so accurately perceive the importance of the people's view of events that in all his actions he was never once untrue to it?
The source of that extraordinary power of penetrating the meaning of the events then occurring lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest human pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be cast in the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has invented.
To a lackey no man can be great, for a lackey has his own conception of greatness.
